text:
Database Management Systems
Path
●A path specifies a traversal of part of the graph.
●It is typically used as part of a query to specify a pattern, where the query will retrieve from the
graph data that matches the pattern.
●A path is typically specified by a start node, followed by one or more relationships, leading to one
or more end nodes that satisfy the pattern.
●It is somewhat similar to the concepts of path expressions in the context of query languages for
object databases (OQL) and XML (XPat and XQuery).

Database Management Systems
Optional Schema
●A schema is optional in Neo4j.
●Graphs can be created and used without a schema, but in Neo4j version 2.0, a few schema-
related functions were added.
●The main features related to schema creation involve creating indexes and constraints
based on the labels and properties.
●For example, it is possible to create the equivalent of a key constraint on a property of a
label, so all nodes in the collection of nodes associated with the label must have unique
values for that property.

text:
Database Management Systems
Indexing and node identifiers
●When a node is created, the Neo4j system creates an internal unique system-defined identifier
for each node.
●To retrieve individual nodes using other properties of the nodes efficiently, the user can create
indexes for the collection of nodes that have a particular label.
●Typically, one or more of the properties of the nodes in that collection can be indexed.
●For example, Empid can be used to index nodes with the EMPLOYEE label, Dno to index the nodes
with the DEPARTMENT label, and Pno to index the nodes with the PROJECT label.

text:
Database Management Systems
Introduction to Vectordatabases
•
To understand why we are moving to vector databases or RDBMS with vector search options. We
need to know about full text search :
•
Full-text search (FTS) is a feature that allows users to efficiently search for words or phrases
within large textual columns (like articles, descriptions, documents) stored in a database. Unlike
simple string pattern matching (using LIKE or regular expressions), full-text search in a DBMS is
designed to handle large volumes of text data and to provide meaningful, relevance-ranked results.
•
Vector search is better than traditional full-text search in DBMS because it retrieves results based on
semantic meaning, not just matching exact words or patterns. It uses high-dimensional
embeddings to find conceptually similar content, naturally handling synonyms, context, and user
intent. This makes it far more effective for modern applications like recommendation systems, question
answering, and multilingual search.

Vector Databases
•
Vector databases have gained significant importance in various
fields due to their unique ability to efficiently store, index, and
search high-dimensional data points, often referred to as vectors.
•
These databases are designed to handle data where each entry is
represented as a vector in a multi-dimensional space.
•
The vectors can represent a wide range of information, such as
numerical features, embeddings from text or images, and even
complex data like molecular structures.
•
Let’s represent the vector database using a 2D grid where one
axis represents the color of the animal (brown, black, white) and
the other axis represents the size (small, medium, large).

text:
Database Management Systems
How does a vector database differ from a traditional database?

Database Management Systems
Vector Database Capabilities
The significance of vector databases lies in their capabilities and applications:
- Efficient Similarity Search:
•
Vector databases excel at performing similarity searches, where you can retrieve vectors that
are most similar to a given query vector.
- High-Dimensional Data:
•
Vector databases are designed to handle high-dimensional data more efficiently, making
them suitable for applications like natural language processing, computer vision, and genomics.
- Machine Learning and AI:
•
Vector databases are often used to store embeddings generated by machine learning models.
These embeddings capture the essential features of the data and can be used for various tasks,
such as clustering, classification, and anomaly detection.

text:

Vector Database Capabilities
Real-time Applications:
Many vector databases are optimized for real-time or near-real-time querying, making them suitable for
applications that require quick responses, such as recommendation systems in e-commerce, fraud
detection, and monitoring IoT sensor data.
Personalization and User Profiling:
Vector databases enable personalized experiences by allowing systems to understand and predict user
preferences. This is crucial in platforms like streaming services, social media, and online marketplaces.
Spatial and Geographic Data:
Vector databases can handle geographic data, such as points, lines, and polygons, efficiently. This is
essential in applications like geographical information systems (GIS), location-based services, and
navigation applications.

text:
Database Management Systems
Q&A
Database Management Systems
Which of the following best describes a primary advantage of vector databases over traditional
relational databases?
A) They store structured tabular data more efficiently
B) They allow faster transaction processing for numeric data
C) They enable similarity searches based on semantic meaning
D) They use B-tree indexes for optimizing join operations
Answer: C
Explanation: Vector databases are designed to perform efficient similarity searches based on high-
dimensional vector embeddings that capture semantic relationships, unlike traditional relational
databases which rely on structured tabular data and exact matches.

Database Management Systems
Q&A
Database Management Systems
In the context of database systems, what does full-text search (FTS) primarily enable?
A) Retrieving documents by matching semantic similarity of content
B) Searching large text columns by tokenizing and indexing words
C) Efficient storage of high-dimensional vectors from machine learning models
D) Generating vector embeddings for text and images
Answer: B
Explanation: Full-text search in traditional DBMS breaks text into tokens (words), builds an
index, and allows searching large text fields efficiently based on exact or normalized word
matches.

B) Performing multilingual similarity search across text documents

text:
Database Management Systems
Understanding Embedding
•
Embedding models help us work out which objects are similar by converting very complex data
(such as text, images, documents or videos) into vectors, which consist of numerical data.
•
Given that we need to quantify which objects are similar, it really helps to have numerical data for
solving this problem.
•
Converting data into vectors is a way of simplifying data, while still retaining the most important
features of it.
•
Words are represented as vectors in a high-dimensional space, where each dimension of the space
corresponds to a specific aspect or feature of the word's meaning.
•
For example, dimensions might represent things like context, semantics, or syntax.
•
The procedure to generate the vectors from words is called embeddings. ( Text, documents,
sentences, chat messages , Images , Audio, Videos. These data types are converted into vector
embeddings )

text:
Database Management Systems
Understanding Embedding
•
Vector embeddings are numerical interpretations that retain the contextual significance of data ,
facilitating the alignment of similar entities within a vector space for similarity searches.
•
Vector embeddings numerically capture the semantic meaning of the objects in relation to other
objects. Thus, similar objects are grouped together in the vector space, which means the closer
two objects are, the more similar they are.
•
For example, closely related concepts like "Boats" and "Ferries" may be positioned near each
other due to their contextual links.

Model

• These models learn from a lot of text to
map words into a multi-dimensional vector
space.

Database Management Systems
Understanding Embedding
•
While the embeddings can be stored as numeric arrays, searching the arrays stored in SQL
databases can be memory-intensive and time-consuming.
•
Every time a search operation needs to be done, all the vectors are retrieved, the cosine
similarity is calculated, and the matching string is returned based on the value of cosine
similarity or distance.
•
The vector length for image, video, and audio data tends to be much bigger than the text data.
•
To address this, most RDBMS systems now provide a wrapper or add-on on top of the existing
RDBMS that allows having a vector as a data type.
•
And allows retrieving the data intrinsically based on the similarity between vectors rather than
manually calculating the distance or cosine similarity.

text:
Database Management Systems
Similarity Score
•
There are various metrics to measure the distance between vector
or data points.
•
Two commonly used metrics are Cosine and Euclidean.
•
In the cosine metric, we determine similarity by calculating the
cosine value of the angle (θ) between two vectors. When the
angle between two vectors is close to zero, the cosine value is close
to 1. Conversely, if the angle is 90 degrees (referred to as
orthogonal vectors in mathematics), the cosine value is zero.

Database Management Systems
Similarity Score
•
We can use Cosine metric to calculate similarity between sentence.
For example,
•
let’s consider a new sentence: “Rainy days make me sad”.
•
If we want to find a sentence with a similar meaning from our existing list of sentences, calculating
the cosine for each sentence provides values like these.
‘Rainy days can be gloomy’ is the most
similar sentence to our new one. Both
convey negative feelings about rain. On
the other hand, ‘Success is rewarding’
yields the smallest cosine value, which
makes sense as it expresses a positive
sentiment.
฀That is precisely the objective with the
vector database, to rapidly identify
similar entries

from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity
sentences = [
"I love machine learning",
"I enjoy studying AI"
]
# Convert sentences to TF-IDF vectors
vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer()
tfidf_matrix = vectorizer.fit_transform(sentences)
# Compute cosine similarity
similarity = cosine_similarity(tfidf_matrix[0:1], tfidf_matrix[1:2])

text:
Database Management Systems
Vector Search in Vector Databases
Database Management Systems
Popular Algorithms for clustering and Indexing
• KNN (K-Nearest Neighbors):
•Finds exact nearest neighbors based on distance
•Good for small to medium datasets
• ANN (Approximate Nearest Neighbors):
•Finds approximate nearest neighbors
•Improves efficiency for large, high-dimensional data
• HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World):
•Builds hierarchical graph structure during indexing
•Enables fast neighbor queries, balancing accuracy & speed
•Used in vector DBs like Azure AI Search for ANN searches

Database Management Systems
Q&A
Which of the following is used to measure similarity
between vectors in vector search?
a) Primary key indexing
b) Cosine similarity
c) Sorting by timestamps
d) Hashing
Answer: b) Cosine similarity
What is a primary benefit of using an HNSW index in vector search?
a) It guarantees exact nearest neighbors with exhaustive search
b) It compresses data using product quantization
c) It builds a hierarchical graph for fast & memory-efficient search
d) It only works for low-dimensional data
Answer: c) It builds a hierarchical graph for fast & memory-efficient search
Which indexing method combines inverted files
with vector compression to achieve high-
accuracy searches on massive datasets?
a) Flat index
b) IVFPQ
c) Vantage-Point Tree
d) HNSW
Answer: b) IVFPQ

text:
Database Management Systems
Introduction
●We have learnt before that NoSQL Databases are primarily used for horizontal scalability and
can store various types of data.
●From the slides previously mentioned we also know vectors are used to represent high
dimensional data.
●Vector search is an essential technique used to find similar items using the concept of vector
embeddings.
●Now since we know that these embedding operations and search operations are computationally
intensive, NoSQL databases, especially in-memory ones like Redis, are built for the low-latency
reads/writes needed to serve real-time results.

Database Management Systems
Why use NoSQL for Vector Search ?
1.
Unified Data Model:
•
NoSQL allows you to store the vector embedding alongside the operational metadata that gives
it context (e.g., product price, user ID).
•
This avoids creating separate databases for vectors and business data, simplifying your
architecture.
2.
Built for AI-Scale:
•
AI applications generate vast amounts of data. Since NoSQL databases have the concept of a
“flexible schema”, it fits perfectly with storing data in AI applications like recommendation
systems.
•
If you are building a RAG system or an LLM chatbot, semantic caching can also be used to
reduce costs and increase performance
3.
Allow use of Hybrid Search Queries:
•
Because the vectors are stored with the rest of your data, you can combine a semantic vector
search with traditional, precise metadata filtering in a single query.

Using Redis NoSQL for Vector Search
Let’s understand how Redis (NoSQL) is used to perform Vector Search:
●Vector search capabilities in Redis are provided by Redis Stack, which bundles Redis with
powerful modules like RediSearch.
●VECTOR, A native, binary-safe data type is used to perform vector comparisons. This is
much faster than storing vectors as text strings.
●Redis also allows you to build indexes that combine VECTOR fields with other data types like
text, numbers, and tags. This is the key to enabling powerful hybrid searches.
●It supports different Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) algorithms to let you choose the
right balance between speed, memory usage, and accuracy for your specific needs.

text:
Database Management Systems
Indexing Methods in Redis
Let’s discuss the two most common indexing methods used in Redis
1.
FLAT (Flat index):
•
How it works: Brute-force search. Compares the query vector to every other vector.
•
Pros: 100% accurate results (Exact Nearest Neighbor).
•
Cons: Slow. O(N) complexity. Only for smaller datasets.
2.
HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World):
•
How it works: Creates a multi-layered graph that allows for very fast traversal to find ANN. It
starts at a high, sparse layer and navigates down to denser layers closer to the target.
•
Pros: Extremely fast (logarithmic complexity), even with billions of vectors.
•
Cons: It's approximate, but recall is typically over 99%. This is the standard choice for most
production systems.

text:
Database Management Systems
Vector Search in Redis
Vector Search in Redis is a 3-step Process
Step 1: Creating an Index Schema by defining the structure, the vector field and its algorithm.

Database Management Systems
Vector Search in Redis
Step 1: Creating an Index Schema by defining the structure, the vector field and its algorithm.
●FT.index is used to create the vector index (idx:user_prefs is the index name)
●JSON data type is used and the index will operate on this data type (Can also use HSET)
●PREFIX 1 means that one prefix is specified, and user means that only keys starting with user:
will be indexed. Example: user:1 is indexed but session:1 is not indexed
●SCHEMA defines the list of fields that Redis should index (Relate it to your columns in a table)
●Each field in the schema has the following things
○$.path which creates the field name by prefixing $. (like your col name)
○Type of the field
●TAG indicates that this field is for exact matching and does not tokenize words (Used for filtering)
●VECTOR HNSW is used to create the vector field using the HSNW indexing algorithm
●TYPE FLOAT 32 makes it a 32 bit floating value
●DIM 3 means the dimensions of the vector is 3
●DISTANCE_METRIC COSINE is used to ensure cosine similarity is used.

●DISTANCE_METRIC COSINE is used to ensure cosine similarity is used.

Step 3: Performing the vector search (semantic search)
●FT.SEARCH is the command from RediSearch module that is used to perform vector search
●idx:user_prefs is the name of the index created
●(*) is called the wildcard search pattern. This is used to match all the documents since we want
to filter by similarity and not by precise text matching or tag matching
●KNN 2 returns the 2 most similar documents to the query
●@vector_embedding is the field name in which we had created the index that stores vector
embeddings
●$input_vector is the parameter placeholder. The data comes from the PARAMS command in the
2nd line
●PARAMS 2 means that there are 2 parameters being passed (name and value)
●input_vector is the placeholder name again
●We then pass the model generated embeddings instead of <> part
●DIALECT 2 lets redis know that we are using vector search in the RediSearch module
